01.event: While Rabbi Elazar sat absorbed in Torah study in Tzippori's lower market, his cloak lay forgotten in the upper market, and a man came to take it.
01.turn: The would-be thief found a serpent lying on the cloak.
01.outcome: The cloak was protected; the man could not take it.
01.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was so absorbed in Torah study that he would sit studying in the lower marketplace of Tzippori while his cloak lay in the upper marketplace. Once a man came to steal the cloak, but found a serpent lying on it, guarding it.

02.actor: Pishon the camel driver and his wife
02.event: The wife of Pishon the camel driver refused (annulled) her marriage to him in his absence.
02.turn: Pishon had mismanaged her property, so the Sages dealt with him by a 'defective measure' in return.
02.outcome: Her refusal in his absence was allowed to stand as a punishment to him.
02.summary: Pishon the camel driver mishandled the property his wife brought into the marriage. When she declared her refusal to remain married to him, it was done in his absence, and the Sages let it stand, measuring him with the same defective measure he had used.
02.missing: The events themselves are only cited in a legal debate; what Pishon actually did and how the annulment proceeded are not narrated.

03.event: Rabbi Shabbtai's widowed daughter-in-law seized a saddlebag full of coins for her sustenance.
03.turn: The Sages tried to take it back from her.
03.outcome: The Sages had no power to remove it from her possession.
03.summary: Rav Dimi reported that Rabbi Shabbtai's daughter-in-law grabbed a saddlebag full of coins to support herself. The Sages found they had no authority to take it back from her, and she kept it.

04.event: Rav arrived at Damharya and issued a practical ruling about a breach in a wall.
04.turn: Rav Hanan bar Rava claimed Rav had only done so because he found an unguarded valley and fenced it in.
04.summary: Rav once came to a place called Damharya and issued a practical ruling there, which Rav Huna cited as support for his view. Rav Hanan bar Rava answered that Rav had acted only because he found an unguarded valley and fenced it in as a special precaution.
04.missing: The incident is only cited as precedent in a legal dispute; what Rav saw and did at Damharya is not told.

06.event: The Rabbis urged Rav Sheshet to marry and have sons, and he answered that his daughter's sons are his sons.
06.turn: His answer was a deflection; the real reason was that he had become impotent from waiting through Rav Huna's long lectures.
06.summary: The Rabbis told Rav Sheshet to marry and father sons. He replied that his daughter's sons counted as his own. The Gemara explains he was only putting them off: he had become impotent from sitting through Rav Huna's lengthy discourses.
06.missing: The outcome (that he did not remarry) is implied, not stated.

07.event: Rav Hinnana bar Shelamiya was teaching a mishna to Hiyya bar Rav in Rav's presence.
07.turn: Rav rebuked him for teaching it according to the lone opinion of Rabbi Meir rather than the Rabbis.
07.summary: Rav Hinnana bar Shelamiya was teaching Rav's son Hiyya a mishna in front of Rav, formulating it in a stringent way. Rav challenged him: had he abandoned the majority of the Rabbis to follow Rabbi Meir?
07.missing: No response or outcome to Rav's rebuke is given; the rest is legal explanation.

08.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
08.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba met Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying his grandson to the synagogue with only a cheap cloth on his head.
08.turn: Asked why such haste, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cited the verse equating teaching one's grandchildren with standing at Sinai.
08.outcome: From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba would not eat breakfast until he had reviewed and added to his child's studies.
08.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba saw Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing his grandchild to study, a cheap covering thrown on his head. When he asked why such a fuss, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi quoted the verse linking teaching one's grandchildren to standing at Sinai. Moved, Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba resolved never to eat breakfast before teaching his child; Rabba bar Rav Huna likewise would not eat before bringing his child to the study hall.

09.actor: A depositor and the estate of Rav Dimi
09.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without leaving instructions about it.
09.turn: The ownership was disputed before Rabbi Abba, who knew Rav Dimi was not wealthy and noted the claimant gave an identifying mark.
09.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded the silk to the claimant.
09.summary: A man left silk in the house of Rav Dimi, Rav Safra's brother, and Rav Dimi died without saying anything about it. The case came before Rabbi Abba, who ruled the silk belonged to the claimant, since Rav Dimi was known to be poor and the claimant could describe a distinguishing mark.

10.event: Reish Lakish demanded proof of priestly status from teruma, and Rabbi Elazar objected that priesthood does not vanish where there is no threshing floor.
10.turn: Later, when the same case came before Rabbi Yohanan, Rabbi Yohanan made the very same objection, revealing that Rabbi Elazar had been quoting him.
10.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing Rabbi Yohanan by name.
10.summary: A man testified before Reish Lakish that someone was a priest because he read first from the Torah. Reish Lakish demanded to know if he had seen him receive teruma, and Rabbi Elazar objected. Later, before Rabbi Yohanan, the same thing happened and Rabbi Yohanan gave Rabbi Elazar's exact objection. Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar: you heard this from the blacksmith's son and didn't tell us it was his?

11.event: A son-in-law passed by the door of his father-in-law's house.
11.turn: There were rumors about him and his mother-in-law.
11.summary: A certain man walked past the entrance of his father-in-law's house, and Rav Sheshet had him flogged. The reason was that there were already rumors of an affair between him and his mother-in-law, and his passing by fed them.
11.missing: The case is cited briefly within a legal discussion; little of the incident itself is told.

13.event: Rav Malkiyyu arranged a marriage for a deaf-mute neighbor and wrote the bride a 400-dinar marriage contract from the man's property.
13.turn: Though the deaf-mute was not obligated to give a marriage contract, Rav Malkiyyu reasoned that a wife served him even better than a maidservant whom the court would buy him.
13.summary: A deaf-mute man lived near Rav Malkiyyu, who married him off and wrote the wife a 400-dinar marriage contract from his property. Rav Malkiyyu reasoned that if the court would buy him a maidservant, all the more so a wife. Rava admired him: who is as wise as Rav Malkiyyu?

16.event: In a shepherds' village an alleyway ending in a backyard was brought before Rav Yehuda for a ruling.
16.outcome: He required nothing further to permit carrying there.
16.summary: Rav Yosef recalled a case in a shepherds' village where an alleyway ended in a backyard. The matter came before Rav Yehuda, who ruled that nothing was needed to permit carrying in it.
16.missing: Only a bare report of a ruling; no development or turn in the incident.

17.actor: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya
17.event: A widow came before Rav Yosef demanding sustenance, then wine, then silk garments.
17.turn: When Rav Yosef asked why she needed silk, she retorted it was for him and his colleagues, so she would not be shamed before them.
17.outcome: Her retort stands as the final word.
17.summary: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of D'vil came to Rav Yosef for support. He granted her food, then wine. When she asked for silk clothes and he asked why, she answered: for you, your friends and your friends' friends, so that she need not be ashamed before the scholars.
17.missing: It is not stated whether Rav Yosef granted the silk.

18.event: While Rabbi Yehuda and others sat before Rabbi Tarfon, a yevama came to perform halitza.
18.turn: Rabbi Tarfon instructed all present to call out 'He who had his shoe removed' three times.
18.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalled sitting before Rabbi Tarfon when a widow came to perform the halitza ceremony. Rabbi Tarfon told everyone present to answer together, three times, 'He who had his shoe removed.'
18.missing: The ceremony's conclusion is not told; the incident is a brief precedent.

19.event: Rav Kahana asked Rav Ashi to testify for him, prompting his memory, but Rav Ashi said he did not remember.
19.turn: Rav Ashi eventually remembered and testified, but Rav Kahana hesitated, fearing he had influenced the testimony.
19.outcome: Rav Ashi assured him he had recalled it through his own effort, not by relying on Rav Kahana.
19.summary: Rav Kahana needed Rav Ashi's testimony and tried to jog his memory, but Rav Ashi insisted he did not remember. Later Rav Ashi recalled the matter and testified. Seeing Rav Kahana uneasy that he had planted the memory, Rav Ashi told him: do you think I am relying on you? I worked at it and remembered on my own.

20.actor: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba, Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi
20.event: Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi were studying when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed by, and they stood for him.
20.turn: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba objected that they were ordained and he was not, and that Torah does not stand before its students.
20.outcome: He told them they need not have stood.
20.summary: Two scholars, Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi, were sitting and studying when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba walked by, and they rose for him. He told them they should not have: they were ordained and he was merely an associate, and besides, the Torah they were studying does not stand up for those who study it.
